content: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is a significant cause of illness and death in the United States. The primary mode of HCV transmission is through parenteral exposure to infectious blood or body fluids containing blood, with injection drug use being the most common risk factor. Currently, there is no vaccine available for HCV, nor are there effective preor post-exposure prophylactic measures. Over half of individuals infected with HCV progress to chronic infection. However, direct-acting antiviral (DAA) treatments can achieve a virologic cure in most patients within 8 to 12 weeks using all-oral medication regimens. HCV is a small, single-stranded RNA virus belonging to the Flavivirus family, characterized by high genetic variability. Seven distinct genotypes of HCV have been identified, with genotype 1 being the most prevalent in the United States and globally. This genetic diversity has implications for treatment, as some therapeutic options are genotype-specific. The virus's high mutation rate contributes to its ability to evade the immune system. Importantly, prior HCV infection does not confer immunity against reinfection with the same or different genotypes. HCV is primarily transmitted through direct percutaneous exposure to blood. While mucous membrane exposure to blood can also result in transmission, it is less efficient. The virus can be detected in saliva, semen, breast milk, and other body fluids, but these are not considered efficient vehicles for transmission. Injection drug use (IDU) is the most common route of HCV transmission in the United States. Other risk factors include unsafe medical practices, such as improper handling of injections or hemodialysis, and certain sexual behaviors, particularly among individuals with HIV. Additional risks include sharing personal items like razors or toothbrushes, unregulated tattooing, needlestick injuries among healthcare workers, and perinatal transmission from an infected mother to her infant. Perinatal transmission of HCV has become increasingly significant due to rising infection rates among women of childbearing age. The risk of perinatal transmission is approximately 5.8% for infants born to mothers with HCV, and this risk doubles if the mother is co-infected with HIV. Transmission is almost exclusively associated with mothers who have detectable HCV RNA. Among infants with perinatally acquired HCV, only about 20% clear the infection spontaneously, while 50% develop chronic asymptomatic infection, and 30% progress to chronic active infection. Liver disease complications in childhood are rare, but fibrosis progression over time can lead to severe disease in young adulthood. Acute HCV infection is often asymptomatic or presents with mild symptoms similar to other types of viral hepatitis. Symptoms, when present, may include anorexia, malaise, or abdominal pain. Fulminant hepatic failure is rare. The average incubation period from exposure to symptom onset is 2 to 12 weeks. HCV antibodies (anti-HCV) typically become detectable 4 to 10 weeks after infection, with 97% of individuals seroconverting within six months. HCV RNA can be detected as early as 1 to 2 weeks post-exposure, indicating active infection. Approximately 15% to 25% of individuals with acute HCV infection clear the virus spontaneously, though recent data suggest this rate may be as high as 46%, depending on factors such as age at infection. Spontaneous clearance is less common in individuals co-infected with HIV. Predictors of spontaneous clearance include jaundice, elevated alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels, female sex, younger age, HCV genotype 1, and certain genetic polymorphisms near the IL28B gene. Chronic HCV infection occurs when the virus evades the host immune response, leading to persistent viral replication. The progression of chronic liver disease is typically insidious, with most individuals remaining asymptomatic for 20 years or more. Over 10 to 20 years, approximately 5% to 25% of individuals with chronic HCV develop cirrhosis, and those with cirrhosis face a 1% to 4% annual risk of hepatocellular carcinoma. Factors associated with accelerated disease progression include male sex, age over 50, alcohol use, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, co-infection with hepatitis B virus (HBV) or HIV, and immunosuppressive therapy. Chronic HCV infection can also manifest with extrahepatic complications, such as membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, essential mixed cryoglobulinemia, porphyria cutanea tarda, and lymphoma. The advent of DAA therapies has revolutionized HCV treatment. These agents are well-tolerated, have shorter treatment durations, and are more effective than older interferon-based regimens. DAAs include protease inhibitors, nucleoside analog polymerase inhibitors, and nonstructural protein inhibitors, many of which are pangenotypic, meaning they are effective against all HCV genotypes. A sustained virologic response (SVR), defined as undetectable HCV RNA 12 weeks after completing treatment, indicates a cure. Approximately 90% of HCV-infected individuals can achieve SVR with 8 to 12 weeks of therapy, regardless of genotype, prior treatment history, fibrosis level, or cirrhosis status. Despite their efficacy, DAAs are not yet approved for use during pregnancy, and safety data in this population are limited. Preliminary studies have not identified safety concerns, but larger studies are needed. Testing for HCV during pregnancy remains beneficial for both mothers and infants, as it allows for early diagnosis and potential linkage to care postpartum. Pregnancy provides a unique opportunity for HCV screening, as many women access healthcare only during this period. Identifying HCV infection during pregnancy can also inform delivery management to reduce the risk of perinatal transmission. Universal HCV screening during pregnancy has been recommended by the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases and the Infectious Diseases Society of America. Testing during pregnancy enables simultaneous identification of infected mothers and infants who require follow-up testing. Infants can be tested for HCV RNA at or after two months of age or for anti-HCV antibodies at or after 18 months. While DAA treatment is not approved for children under three years of age, infected children should be monitored. DAAs have been approved for use in older children, with ledipasvir/sofosbuvir approved for those aged three years and older and glecaprevir/pibrentasvir approved for those aged 12 years and older. HCV infection is not an indication for cesarean delivery and does not contraindicate breastfeeding, provided the mother's nipples are not bleeding or cracked. However, certain delivery practices, such as avoiding internal fetal monitoring and prolonged rupture of membranes, may reduce the risk of perinatal transmission. Efforts to eliminate HCV as a public health problem in the United States face substantial challenges. Universal screening and improved access to DAA treatment are critical to achieving this goal. Strengthened guidance for universal HCV testing and strategies to address barriers to care are necessary to ensure healthcare equity and the success of expanded screening initiatives.
